chats.title: RD design for class size caps

messages.text: I'm setting up a regression discontinuity project on class size. The district data I have uses a maximum class size of 30, so when a grade cohort hits 31 students the school has to split into two classes and average class size drops sharply. I want to use enrolment as the running variable and estimate the effect on end-of-year test scores. I know the basic fuzzy RD setup, but I'm wondering how people usually handle multiple cutoffs at 30, 60, 90 in one model.

With multiple cutoffs, the common approaches are either to normalise the running variable relative to the nearest threshold and pool, or to estimate each cutoff separately and then combine. Pooling gains power but assumes the effect is similar at each cutoff, which may not hold since going from 30 to 15.5 students is a much bigger proportional change than going from 90 to 22.5. A useful middle ground is to use predicted class size from the cap rule as the instrument for actual class size, which naturally scales the first stage at each cutoff. You can then check heterogeneity by estimating cutoff-specific local effects and seeing whether they line up.

That makes sense. I'm leaning toward the predicted class size instrument, since the first stage is going to be fuzzy anyway. Some schools split early at 28 or 29, and some ask for exemptions and run a class of 32. My plan is to use local linear regression with a triangular kernel and MSE-optimal bandwidths, and cluster at the school level. Does clustering by school make sense when the variation is at the grade-cohort level?

Clustering at the school level is usually the safer choice. Cohorts within the same school share teachers, administrators, and policies on splitting classes, so their errors are probably correlated. Clustering only at the grade-cohort level could understate your standard errors. If you have few schools, think about wild cluster bootstrap. Also, with a discrete running variable like enrolment counts, it is worth checking robustness to the discreteness, for example by looking at how sensitive estimates are to bandwidth choice and reporting results across a range of bandwidths, not just the optimal one.

Random question, totally outside my field. I was reading about knot theory over the weekend and learned that the Jones polynomial is a knot invariant but it doesn't distinguish all knots. I get that an invariant means equivalent knots give the same polynomial. But why would two genuinely different knots end up with the same Jones polynomial? Is there some intuition for what information the polynomial throws away? It feels like it should be a fingerprint.

Good question. The Jones polynomial is computed from local crossing information through the skein relation, which relates a knot to two simpler diagrams obtained by changing or smoothing one crossing. That recursion captures a lot, but it is essentially a linear combination over states, and different global structures can sum to the same result. A classic source of collisions is mutation: cut out a tangle with four endpoints, rotate it, and glue it back. Mutants are often genuinely different knots, but the Jones polynomial provably cannot tell them apart. So it loses some information about how pieces are arranged globally.

Oh interesting, so it's kind of blind to that rotation operation by construction. That's a bit like an estimator that is invariant to some transformation and therefore can't identify a parameter. Is there anything that does fully distinguish knots, or is that an open problem? And is it still unknown whether the Jones polynomial detects the unknot? I think I saw that mentioned somewhere and found it surprising.

Your analogy is apt: mutation is like a symmetry the invariant cannot see, so it is not identified. Complete invariants do exist in a theoretical sense, for example the knot group together with peripheral structure distinguishes knots up to mirror images, but they are not easy to compute or compare. On the unknot question, you remembered correctly. Whether a nontrivial knot can have the same Jones polynomial as the unknot is still open. Khovanov homology, a richer invariant that categorifies the Jones polynomial, is known to detect the unknot, which makes the open question even more intriguing.

Big worry in my class size project. If principals know the cap is 30, they might push enrolment around near the threshold. For example, a school with 31 kids might discourage one family or delay a transfer so they don't have to hire another teacher. Or some parents might deliberately pick schools just above the cutoff to get smaller classes. Either way the running variable is manipulated. How do I test for this convincingly?

Start with a density test of the running variable at each cutoff. A classic density discontinuity test or the newer local polynomial density estimators will tell you whether there is bunching just below 30 or a gap just above it. Second, check covariate balance: prior test scores, share of low-income students, and parental education should be smooth through the cutoff. Third, think about timing. If enrolment is measured at a fixed date before schools can respond, manipulation is harder. Using an earlier enrolment measure, such as spring registrations, as the running variable can help.

I ran a quick density check and there's a visible pile-up at 29 and 30 and a dip at 31 and 32. Not huge but definitely there, and it's worse in schools with tight budgets. I'm thinking of using a donut RD that drops observations right at the threshold, and also using the previous year's projected enrolment as an instrument. I'm unsure whether the donut is enough or whether it just throws away the most informative observations.

Your concern is valid. A donut RD only helps if manipulation is limited to observations right next to the cutoff. If schools near 33 also move students, the donut does not fix the problem, and you pay in precision and more extrapolation. Projected enrolment is a stronger idea if projections are made before schools can act strategically. You could also bound the effect, for example by trimming the excess mass below the cutoff in the most and least favourable ways. The heterogeneity by budget pressure is interesting in itself and may be worth reporting as evidence about the mechanism.

I've been thinking about maps lately. Everybody knows Mercator makes Greenland look as large as Africa, yet it's still the default in classrooms and on web maps. Why does it persist? And I'm curious whether growing up with Mercator actually distorts people's mental maps of the world, like do people really think northern countries are bigger? It seems like something you could measure, but I don't know if anyone has done it carefully.

Mercator persists for a few reasons. It is conformal, so it preserves local angles and shapes, which made it ideal for navigation and now for web maps, where zooming into a street should not distort its shape. Web mapping tools adopted a variant of it because square tiles at every zoom level are easy to compute. Inertia matters too: textbooks and wall maps reuse familiar images. On mental maps, there is research where people draw or estimate country sizes, and many overestimate high-latitude regions and underestimate Africa, though disentangling Mercator exposure from other factors is tricky.

That's the part that interests me as an empirical person. You'd need some variation in exposure to Mercator that isn't correlated with everything else. Maybe classrooms that switched wall maps to an equal-area projection at some point? I'm not going to pursue it, but I'm curious how big the distortion is. Do people also misjudge distances, or is it mostly area?

A curriculum change like that would be a natural experiment, though you would need to measure perceptions before and after. Studies suggest the area errors are the most consistent, especially overestimating Europe and North America relative to Africa and South America. Distance estimates are distorted too, but people tend to rely on travel time and other cues as well, so the projection effect is weaker. Interestingly, some research finds people's mental maps are not consistent with any single projection; they are a patchwork that blends map exposure, familiarity, and how culturally central a region feels.

chats.title: First stage too weak at upper cutoffs

messages.text: Update on the class size RD. The first stage looks great at the 30 cutoff, predicted class size jumps and actual class size follows closely. But at 60 and 90 the first stage is much weaker, because larger schools apparently have more flexibility with mixed-grade classes and teaching assistants. The F-statistics there are around 6 or 7. Should I just drop the upper cutoffs, or is there a way to use them without weak-instrument problems?

Weak first stages at the upper cutoffs are common in this kind of design. You have several options. First, report the estimates for the first cutoff as the main result and present the others as secondary, using weak-instrument-robust inference such as confidence intervals based on inverting a weak-IV-robust test. Second, if you pool cutoffs, the strong first stage at 30 can carry the joint estimate, but then the estimate mostly reflects the first cutoff. Third, think about whether the weaker compliance at higher cutoffs is itself informative about how schools respond to the rule.

I like the weak-IV-robust confidence interval approach. My bigger concern is interpretation: at 30 the compliers are mostly small rural schools, and those are different from the urban schools around 60 and 90. So even if I pool, the LATE is really about small schools. I want to be upfront that this design can't say much about class size reductions in large urban schools, which is unfortunately where the policy debate is.

That is a careful point and worth stating clearly in the paper. RD estimates are local both to the cutoff and to the compliers at that cutoff, so external validity is limited. You could describe the complier characteristics at each threshold to make this concrete, comparing school size, urbanicity, and student demographics. If you want to say something about larger schools, you might pair the RD with another source of variation, such as a policy change in caps, or use the covariates to reweight the estimates toward the urban population, while being clear about the extra assumptions.

Out of curiosity, I've been reading about quantum computing and keep running into the claim that you need something like a thousand physical qubits for every logical qubit with surface codes. Why is the overhead so huge? I understand classical error correction in a basic way, like repetition codes. What makes quantum error correction so much more expensive, and is it really specific to surface codes or is it more fundamental?

Part of it is fundamental and part is specific to surface codes. Quantum errors are continuous and come in two types, bit flips and phase flips, and you cannot copy or directly measure the state to check it. So you have to measure parity checks using extra ancilla qubits, which themselves make errors. The surface code is popular because it only needs nearest-neighbour interactions on a 2D grid and tolerates fairly high error rates, around one percent. The price is that it encodes just one logical qubit per patch, and the patch size grows with the code distance needed to suppress errors to useful levels.

So the overhead is basically a trade-off: easy-to-build local connectivity in exchange for poor encoding rate. That's kind of elegant. If physical error rates drop a lot, does the overhead fall quickly? And I've heard of other codes, like LDPC codes, that are more efficient. Why isn't everyone using those if they need fewer qubits?

Yes, that captures it. When physical error rates fall further below threshold, the needed code distance drops, and overhead falls substantially, since logical error rates decrease exponentially with distance. Quantum LDPC codes can encode many logical qubits in one block with much better rates. The catch is that they generally require long-range connections between qubits, which are hard to build on planar chips. Some hardware platforms, like neutral atoms or trapped ions, can move qubits around, so they are more promising for these codes. Decoding and implementing logical gates on LDPC codes are also less mature.

Working on robustness for the class size paper. Reviewers in education econ always ask for placebo cutoffs, so I plan to estimate fake discontinuities at enrolments of 20, 25, 40, and 45 where nothing should happen. I'm also going to show the bandwidth sensitivity plot. Anything else I'm missing? I'd like the robustness section to really address the manipulation concern, since that's what I expect people to push hardest on.

Placebo cutoffs and bandwidth sensitivity are standard and good. Additional checks to consider: placebo outcomes, such as test scores from the year before the class assignment, which should not jump at the cutoff; covariate balance tables at each threshold; and estimates that use only schools with no evidence of bunching. For manipulation specifically, you could show that results are similar when using the earlier projected enrolment as the running variable, and include the bounding exercise. A heterogeneity check by budget pressure would also help connect the manipulation evidence to your main results.

Good call on lagged test scores as a placebo outcome, I hadn't planned that. Splitting by bunching is tricky though, because bunching is a school-level behaviour and those schools probably differ in other ways too. I think I'll present it as descriptive rather than causal. I also want to add a sentence on whether the cap rule has been enforced consistently over time, since enforcement got stricter after a funding change.

Presenting the bunching split as descriptive is sensible; you avoid overclaiming while still showing that the results hold where manipulation looks minimal. The enforcement change is worth more than a sentence if you have the data. A stricter cap after the funding change would mean a sharper first stage in later years, and comparing estimates before and after could serve as a check on whether the effect is stable. If enforcement also reduced manipulation, the density test should show less bunching in later years, which would be a nice piece of supporting evidence.

chats.title: Comparing carbon estimates for ML training

messages.text: I keep seeing headlines about the carbon footprint of training large language models, with numbers that vary by orders of magnitude. As someone who does applied empirical work, I'm skeptical whether these figures are even comparable. Different papers seem to use different assumptions about hardware, data centre efficiency, and the electricity grid. Is there a standard methodology, or is everyone kind of making up their own accounting?

Your skepticism is justified. Most estimates multiply energy use by a carbon intensity factor, but choices vary at each step. Energy can come from measured power draw or be estimated from hardware specs and runtime. Data centre overhead, usually captured by power usage effectiveness, ranges from about 1.1 to 1.6. Carbon intensity depends on location and whether you use annual grid averages, hourly marginal emissions, or claimed renewable purchases. Some studies include hyperparameter tuning and failed runs, others count only the final run. Embodied emissions from manufacturing hardware are often excluded entirely.

So it's like comparing treatment effects across studies with different outcome definitions. A meta-analysis would need to harmonise everything first. I'd be curious whether someone could reconstruct a comparable estimate from published details, at least for the bigger models. Is the reporting detailed enough for that? And do inference costs end up mattering more than training once a model is deployed widely?

Reconstruction is possible for some models, since papers often report GPU type, count, and training hours, but location and grid mix are frequently missing, and those can change results by a factor of five or more. Researchers have proposed reporting checklists to make this standard, but adoption is uneven. On inference, for widely used models, cumulative inference energy can exceed training energy over the deployment lifetime, though this depends heavily on usage volume and efficiency. That makes training-only comparisons a partial picture, which is another reason headline figures can mislead.

chats.title: Writing up mechanisms for class size effects

messages.text: Almost done with the class size RD. Main result: a reduction of about five students raises math scores by 0.1 standard deviations, with smaller effects for reading. Now I want to talk about mechanisms. I have teacher surveys on time spent on individual instruction and on discipline, but only for a subset of schools. I worry that using a mediator in the RD framework means I'm sneaking in extra assumptions. How should I frame this?

You are right to be careful. The RD identifies the total effect of class size, but splitting it into mediated pathways requires additional assumptions, such as no unobserved confounding between mediators and outcomes, which the design does not deliver. One honest approach is to estimate the RD effect of class size on each mediator as an outcome itself. That tells you smaller classes change teacher time use, without claiming how much of the score effect runs through it. Also check that the survey subset is balanced around the cutoffs, otherwise selection into the survey could bias things.

Yes, I'll treat the mediators as outcomes and not run any decomposition. The survey subset is mostly from the earlier years, before the enforcement change, so I'll have to note that. Honestly I'm also thinking about a follow-up where I combine this with administrative data on teacher turnover, because smaller classes might help retain teachers, which would be a longer-run channel nobody seems to measure well.

That follow-up sounds promising. Teacher retention is plausibly affected by class size through workload and job satisfaction, and administrative data would let you track it over several years. The same RD design could work with turnover as an outcome, though you would need to think about how teacher assignment interacts with class splits. For example, schools that split a class may hire newer teachers, which mechanically affects turnover. Separating the effect on incumbent teachers from the composition effect of new hires would make the analysis much more convincing.

Non-work question. I've kept a sourdough starter for about a year and I'm fascinated that after the first couple of chaotic weeks, it settles into a stable community. Early on it smelled weird and rose unpredictably, then it became consistent. What's actually happening? Why do the yeast and bacteria reach a stable mix instead of one taking over or the whole thing drifting randomly forever?

Early on, flour and the environment bring in many microbes, including bacteria that do well at neutral pH. As lactic acid bacteria grow, they acidify the starter, which kills off many of those early colonisers. That is the strange smell phase. Once the pH is low, only acid-tolerant species thrive, typically a few lactic acid bacteria and one or two yeasts. Regular feeding resets resources but keeps the same selective conditions, so the community repeatedly converges on the same mix. The yeasts and bacteria also partly use different sugars, which reduces direct competition.

So it's a kind of environmental filtering with periodic disturbance. That makes me wonder how much of the final community depends on the flour versus the baker's hands or kitchen. If two people started starters from the same flour in different kitchens, would they converge to the same thing? It seems like a cute natural experiment, though I suspect people have looked at it.

People have studied this. Comparisons of starters made from the same flour by different bakers suggest the flour contributes many of the microbes, but the baker's hands and environment also leave detectable signatures, and the feeding schedule and temperature strongly shape the final balance. So starters from the same flour often converge to similar but not identical communities. Temperature in particular shifts the ratio of yeast to bacteria and the balance of lactic and acetic acid, which is why the same starter can taste different in summer and winter.
